title: Grade 6 Math Lab
blurb: 14 topics. Each one is a short lesson you can see, then puzzles to try.

tracks.name: Big ideas
tracks.blurb: Real mathematics. A trick a nine-year-old invented, a puzzle that is provably impossible, and a question open since 1742.

tracks.name: Number skills
tracks.blurb: Negatives, ratios, exponents and the start of algebra.

topics.name: Gauss's Trick
topics.big: Add 1 to 100 in about five seconds.
topics.recap: The trick: fold the list. Pair the first number with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on. Every pair adds to the same total.
topics.parentNote: The story is that Gauss, aged about nine, was set this as busywork and answered almost immediately. The pairing argument generalises to n(n+1)/2, which is the handshake formula from grade 1 arriving in algebraic form.

teach.text: Add every number from 1 to 100. Most people start plodding.
Instead, fold the list. Pair the first with the last.

teach.cap: Every pair makes 101. There are 50 pairs.

teach.text: 50 pairs of 101 is 5,050. Done.
The story goes that Gauss did this at about nine years old, while his class was still adding.

exercises.why: 101, and so does 2 + 99, and 3 + 98. Every pair from the outside in gives the same total.

exercises.ask: How many pairs are there in 1 to 100?
exercises.why: 50. A hundred numbers folded in half gives fifty pairs, with nothing left over.
5050. That is the sum of every number from 1 to 100, and the whole job took two multiplications.

exercises.ask: Now use the pairing trick on 1 to 10. Pair 1 with 10, 2 with 9, and so on. What is the total?
exercises.why: 55. Five pairs of 11. And 55 is a triangle number, the same ones from the handshake puzzle.

exercises.ask: Add 1 to 20.
exercises.why: 210. Ten pairs of 21. The rule is: how many, times one more than how many, halved.

exercises.ask: The trick still works when there is an odd count, like 1 to 9.
exercises.why: True. 1 to 9 pairs into four 10s with the 5 left in the middle, so 40 and 5 is 45. The middle number is always half of the pair total.

exercises.ask: Add 1 to 30 using the pairing trick.
exercises.why: 465. Fifteen 31s. The general rule is n times (n+1) divided by 2, and that is exactly the handshake formula wearing algebra.

topics.name: The Broken Board
topics.big: Two squares missing, and now it is impossible.
topics.parentNote: The mutilated chessboard. The colouring argument is a complete, airtight impossibility proof that a child can hold entirely in their head, which is rare and worth meeting.

teach.text: A chessboard has 64 squares. A domino covers exactly 2.
32 dominoes cover it perfectly. Easy.
Now cut off two opposite corners. 62 squares left, so 31 dominoes should fit.

teach.cap: The two missing corners are both the same colour.

teach.text: Every domino covers one of each colour. Always. No exceptions.
You removed two of the same colour, so 30 of one and 32 of the other are left. No arrangement can ever work.

exercises.ask: How many squares on a chessboard?
exercises.why: 64, an 8 by 8 grid. Half are dark and half are light, so 32 each.

exercises.ask: How many squares does one domino cover?
exercises.why: 2, and here is the key: always one dark and one light, because neighbouring squares never match.

exercises.ask: Cut off 2 corners. How many squares are left?
exercises.why: 62. So 31 dominoes would be exactly the right number, which is what makes the puzzle feel possible.

exercises.ask: Opposite corners are the same colour. How many of that colour remain?
exercises.why: 30, with 32 of the other. Once the counts differ, the puzzle is dead.

exercises.ask: 31 dominoes can cover the board with two opposite corners removed.
exercises.why: False, and not because nobody has found a way. 31 dominoes must cover 31 of each colour, and only 30 of one colour exist. It is impossible, proved.

exercises.ask: If you remove two corners of DIFFERENT colours, it becomes possible.
exercises.why: True. With 31 of each colour left it can always be done. The colouring is not just an excuse, it is exactly what decides it.

exercises.ask: Draw an 8 by 8 grid, colour it like a chessboard, cross out two opposite corners. How many dark squares are left?
exercises.hint: Opposite corners always share a colour. Count carefully.
exercises.why: 30. Try to cover it with dominoes and you will always be left with two squares of the same colour, far apart. The counting told you that before you started.

topics.name: Minus Times Minus
topics.big: Why does taking away a debt make you richer?
topics.parentNote: MA.6.NSO.4.2. Most children are told the rule and never shown a reason. The pattern argument is a genuine one, and the debt story makes it concrete.

teach.text: Watch the pattern. 3 x 3 is 9, 3 x 2 is 6, 3 x 1 is 3, 3 x 0 is 0.

teach.cap: Each step down subtracts 3. Carry on past zero.

teach.text: So 3 x -1 must be -3. The pattern gives us no choice.
Now fix the -1 and count down the other side: -1 x 3 is -3, -1 x 2 is -2, -1 x 1 is -1, -1 x 0 is 0.
Each step now ADDS 1, so -1 x -1 has to be 1. Or: taking away a debt of £5 leaves you £5 better off.

exercises.why: -6. Three lots of a debt of two is a debt of six.
12. Removing four debts of three leaves you twelve better off, so it must be positive.
-4. Start seven below zero and climb three. Adding and multiplying follow different rules, which is where most slips happen.
8. Taking away a debt of three makes you three better off, so it is the same as adding.

exercises.ask: A negative times a negative is always positive.
exercises.why: True. It is forced by the pattern: if it were anything else, arithmetic would stop working consistently.
-8. The first two make 4, then times -2 gives -8. An odd number of minus signs leaves a minus.

exercises.ask: Work out -1 x -1 x -1 x -1 on paper.
exercises.hint: Do them two at a time.
exercises.why: 1. Four minus signs, an even number, so they cancel in pairs. Count the minus signs: even gives plus, odd gives minus.

topics.name: Goldbach's Guess
topics.big: Every even number is two primes added. Probably.
topics.parentNote: Goldbach's conjecture, written in a letter in 1742 and still open. It has been checked by computer past four quintillion. A child can test it in a notebook and be doing exactly what everybody else has managed.

teach.text: Take any even number bigger than 2. Try to write it as two primes added.
Christian Goldbach wrote this in a letter in 1742.
Computers have checked past four quintillion. It always works.
Nobody has proved it. You can test it in a notebook and you are doing exactly what everyone else has managed: checking.

exercises.why: 7. Both 5 and 7 are prime, so 12 works.
13, and both are prime. 18 also works as 7 + 11, so some numbers have several ways.
17. Also 7 + 13. The bigger the even number, the more ways there usually are.

exercises.ask: How many ways can 10 be written as two primes? (3+7 and 5+5)
exercises.why: 2. Order does not count as different, so 3+7 and 7+3 are the same way.

exercises.ask: Somebody has proved Goldbach's guess.
exercises.why: False. It has stood since 1742. Every even number anyone has ever tested works, and nobody can show it must.
17. Also 5 + 23. Notice 28 turns up here and as a perfect number in grade 3, for completely unrelated reasons.

exercises.ask: Find two primes that add to 50.
exercises.hint: Try 3 first, then 7, then 13. Type the bigger prime you find.
exercises.why: 3 + 47 works, and so do 7 + 43, 13 + 37 and 19 + 31. Four different ways for one number, and still nobody can prove it never fails.

topics.name: The Birthday Surprise
topics.big: 23 people, and it is better than even odds.
topics.parentNote: The birthday problem. The trick to seeing it is counting pairs rather than people, which is the handshake number from grade 1 turning up in probability.

teach.text: How many people before two share a birthday, more likely than not?
Most people guess about 180. The answer is 23.
The trick is that it is not about you. It is about PAIRS.

teach.cap: The handshake numbers again. 23 people make 253 pairs.

teach.text: 253 chances for a match, not 23. That is why it happens so much sooner than it feels like it should.

exercises.ask: How many pairs can 4 people make?
exercises.why: 6, the handshake number. Everyone pairs with everyone else exactly once.

exercises.ask: How many pairs can 5 people make?
exercises.why: 10. Each new person pairs with everyone already there, so the count climbs fast.

exercises.ask: How many pairs can 10 people make?
exercises.why: 45, from 9 + 8 + 7 + ... + 1. Ten people, but forty-five chances of a match.

exercises.ask: How many days in a year, ignoring leap years?
exercises.why: 365. It feels like you would need hundreds of people, and the pairs are why you do not.

exercises.ask: In a class of 30 it is more likely than not that two share a birthday.
exercises.why: True, about 70% likely. 30 people make 435 pairs, and that many chances is plenty.

exercises.ask: 23 people. How many pairs? (23 x 22 ÷ 2)
exercises.why: 253. That is the number that matters, not 23. Once you count pairs, the answer stops feeling strange.

exercises.ask: Ask 25 people their birth month. Did two share? Type the number of pairs 25 people make.
exercises.why: 300 pairs. With only 12 months, sharing a month is almost certain. This is the pigeonhole principle from grade 1 and the birthday problem meeting up.

topics.name: Shadows and Pyramids
topics.big: Measure a pyramid with a stick.
topics.parentNote: Thales measuring the Great Pyramid by its shadow, around 600 BC. Grade 6 does ratios and unit rates (MA.6.AR.3.x), which is exactly the machinery this needs.

teach.text: At one moment of the day, your shadow is exactly as long as you are tall.
At that moment, every shadow is as long as the thing casting it.
So measure the pyramid's shadow and you have measured the pyramid.
Thales is said to have done this about 2,600 years ago.
Even at other times it works. If your shadow is twice your height, so is everything else's.

exercises.ask: A 2 m stick casts a 2 m shadow. A tree casts 12 m. How tall is the tree?
exercises.why: 12 m. Shadow equals height for everything at that moment, so the tree's shadow is its height.

exercises.ask: A 2 m stick casts a 4 m shadow. A tree casts 20 m. How tall?
exercises.why: 10 m. Shadows are double, so the tree is half its shadow.

exercises.ask: A 1 m stick casts 3 m. A tower casts 45 m. How tall?
exercises.why: 15 m. The shadow is 3 times the height, so divide by 3. That 3 is the unit rate.

exercises.ask: The ratio height to shadow is 1 to 4. A shadow is 32 m. How tall?
exercises.why: 8 m. Divide by 4. Once you have the ratio you can measure anything you can see the shadow of.

exercises.ask: This works for a building you cannot climb.
exercises.why: True, and that is exactly the point. Thales measured the Great Pyramid without going anywhere near the top.

exercises.ask: A 3 m pole casts 1 m of shadow. A wall casts 4 m. How tall?
exercises.why: 12 m. Here the height is 3 times the shadow, so a short shadow means a very tall wall. The sun is high.

exercises.ask: Measure your height and your shadow outside. Then measure a tree's shadow. Type your shadow in whole metres.
exercises.hint: Do both at the same time of day or the ratio changes. Type 1 if your shadow is about a metre.
exercises.why: Whatever you measured, divide the tree's shadow by yours and multiply by your height. That is the tree, without a ladder.

topics.name: Why 60 Minutes?
topics.big: 60 splits more ways than any small number.
topics.parentNote: Why the Babylonians counted in sixties, and why we still do for time and angles. Grade 6 does factors, GCF and LCM (MA.6.NSO.3.1), so this is a factor-counting question with a 4,000-year-old answer.

teach.text: Why 60 minutes and not 100? Because 60 splits beautifully.

teach.cap: All twelve numbers that divide 60 exactly.

teach.text: 60 splits into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths. 100 cannot do thirds.
The Babylonians counted in sixties about 4,000 years ago. We still do, for time and for angles.
360 degrees in a circle is 6 sixties. That is not a coincidence either.

exercises.ask: How many numbers divide 60 exactly?
A third of 60 is?
exercises.why: 20 minutes. A third of an hour is a whole number of minutes, which is why 60 is so convenient.

exercises.ask: How many numbers divide 100 exactly?
exercises.why: 9: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50 and 100. Fewer than 60, even though 100 is bigger.

exercises.ask: A third of 100 is a whole number.
exercises.why: False, it is 33.33 recurring. If an hour had 100 minutes, a third of an hour would be a mess.

exercises.ask: 60 as a product of primes: 2 x 2 x 3 x ?
exercises.why: 5. So 60 is 2 squared times 3 times 5. Having three different small primes is what gives it so many factors.

exercises.ask: How many sixties in 360?
exercises.why: 6. A circle is 360 degrees precisely because 360 splits even more ways than 60 does: it has 24 factors.

exercises.ask: List every factor of 24. How many are there?
exercises.hint: Work in pairs: 1 and 24, 2 and 12, 3 and 8, 4 and 6.
exercises.why: 8. Factors come in pairs, which is why counting them in pairs is quicker and safer than hunting one at a time.

topics.name: Function Machines
topics.big: Feed numbers in. Work out what it does.
topics.recap: A function machine does the same thing to every number you put in. Work out the rule and you can say what comes out of any number.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.AR.1.1 and 1.3. A function as a machine, and finding a rule from its behaviour, which is what algebra is actually for.

teach.text: A machine takes a number in and gives one back.
Put in 1, get 4. Put in 2, get 7. Put in 3, get 10.

teach.cap: Each step in adds 3 to the out. So it multiplies by 3.

teach.text: Multiply by 3 and add 1. Check it: 3 times 3 is 9, plus 1 is 10.
Two things to find: how much it climbs each step, and where it starts. Then write it as 3n + 1.

exercises.ask: The rule is 3n + 1. What comes out when 5 goes in?
exercises.why: 16. Three fives is 15, plus 1.

exercises.askFor: What comes out when 20 goes in?
exercises.ask: Find the rule, then say what 20 gives.
exercises.why: 45. The rule is double and add 5. Each step in raises the out by 2, and putting in 0 would give 5.

exercises.askFor: What comes out when 10 goes in?
exercises.ask: Find this rule, then say what 10 gives.
exercises.why: 37. The rule is times 4, take away 3. Feeding in 0 shows the -3 immediately.

exercises.askFor: What comes out when 12 goes in?
exercises.ask: This one is not a straight line. What does 12 give?
exercises.why: 144. It squares the input. The gaps between outputs grow, which is the sign that it is not multiply-and-add.

exercises.ask: In goes 1, 2, 3. Out comes 5, 10, 15. What is the rule? Type the multiplier.
exercises.why: 5. It multiplies by 5 and adds nothing. Putting in 0 would give 0.

exercises.ask: If the outputs go up by the same amount each time, the rule is multiply and add.
exercises.why: True. A steady climb means multiplying by that climb. If the climb itself changes, something more is going on, like squaring.

exercises.ask: In goes 0, 1, 2, 3. Out comes 7, 10, 13, 16. Write the rule and use it on 100.
exercises.hint: It climbs by 3, and starts at 7.
exercises.why: 307. The rule is 3n + 7, so 300 plus 7. Once you have the rule, the size of the number stops mattering.

topics.name: Below Zero
topics.big: Numbers on the other side of zero.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.NSO.1.1 to 1.4 and 4.1. Negative numbers, opposites and absolute value as distance from zero.

teach.text: A number line does not stop at zero. It carries on the other way.

teach.cap: -2 and 2 are opposites. Both are 2 away from zero.

teach.text: How far from zero is called the absolute value. It is never negative.
-7 is smaller than -2, even though 7 is bigger than 2. Further left means smaller.

exercises.why: 3. Start five below zero and climb eight, so you pass zero and land three above.
-7. Start three below and go four further down.

exercises.ask: What is the absolute value of -9?
exercises.why: 9. Absolute value is distance from zero, and distance is never negative.
-4. You run out of room above zero and carry on four below.

exercises.ask: Which is smallest?
exercises.why: -7. Furthest left on the number line means smallest, even though 7 looks like the biggest digit.

exercises.ask: -2 is bigger than -5.
exercises.why: True. -2 is further right, so it is bigger. A debt of 2 is better than a debt of 5.

exercises.ask: The temperature is -6 and rises 15 degrees. What is it now?
exercises.hint: Six degrees gets you to zero, then keep going.
exercises.why: 9. Six of the rise is used getting to zero, and the other nine take you above it.

topics.name: Ratios and Rates
topics.big: How two amounts compare, and per one.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.AR.3.1 to 3.5. Ratios, unit rates and percentages as a single idea seen from three angles.

teach.text: A ratio compares two amounts. 3 red to 2 blue is written 3:2.
A unit rate says how much for ONE. 12 pounds for 4 kg is 3 pounds per kg.

teach.cap: Equivalent ratios. Every column is the same comparison.

teach.text: A percentage is just a ratio out of 100. 25% means 25 for every 100.

exercises.ask: 12 pounds for 4 kg. What is the cost of 1 kg?
exercises.why: 3 pounds per kg. Divide by how many you had to reach one.

exercises.ask: 3 red to 2 blue. If there are 9 red, how many blue?
exercises.why: 6. The 3 tripled to 9, so the 2 triples to 6. Both sides scale together.

exercises.ask: What is 25% of 80?
exercises.why: 20. 25% is a quarter, and a quarter of 80 is 20.

exercises.ask: A car goes 150 km in 3 hours. How far in 1 hour?
exercises.why: 50 km per hour. Divide by 3 to get the rate for one.

exercises.ask: 15 out of 60 as a percentage.
exercises.why: 25%. 15 out of 60 is a quarter, and a quarter of 100 is 25.

exercises.ask: The ratio 4:6 is the same as 2:3.
exercises.why: True. Divide both by 2 and the comparison does not change, exactly like equivalent fractions.

exercises.ask: A recipe for 4 people uses 200 g of rice. How much for 6 people?
exercises.hint: Find the amount for one person first.
exercises.why: 300 g. 50 g each, times 6. Going through the unit rate always works, even when the numbers do not divide nicely.

topics.name: Powers
topics.big: A short way to write repeated multiplying.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.NSO.3.3 and 3.4. Exponents, and prime factorisation written with them.

teach.text: 2 to the power 5 means 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2, which is 32.

teach.cap: Each step is one more power of 2.

teach.text: The small number counts how many are multiplied, not what you multiply by.
Anything to the power 0 is 1. Going down the chain you halve each time, and half of 2 is 1.

exercises.ask: 2 to the power 5 = ?
exercises.why: 32. Five 2s multiplied. This is the same doubling chain as the Tower of Hanoi.

exercises.ask: 3 to the power 3 = ?
exercises.why: 27. Three 3s: 3 times 3 is 9, times 3 again is 27.

exercises.ask: 10 to the power 4 = ?
exercises.why: 10000. The power counts the zeros, which is why powers of ten are so easy.

exercises.ask: 5 squared = ?
exercises.why: 25. Squared means to the power 2, and it is called that because it is the area of a square with side 5.

exercises.ask: 24 as primes is 2 x 2 x 2 x 3. What power of 2 is in it?
exercises.why: 3. So 24 is 2 cubed times 3. Exponents make prime factorisation much shorter to write.

exercises.ask: 2 to the power 3 is the same as 3 to the power 2.
exercises.why: False. 2 cubed is 8 and 3 squared is 9. The order matters, unlike ordinary multiplication.

exercises.ask: Write 72 as a product of primes. What power of 2 does it have?
exercises.why: 3. 72 is 2 cubed times 3 squared. Halving three times gets you to 9, which is 3 squared.

topics.name: Letters for Numbers
topics.big: A letter stands for a number you do not know yet.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.AR.1.1 to 1.4 and 2.2 to 2.3. Writing expressions, substituting, and solving one-step equations.

teach.text: 'Five more than a number' is written n + 5.
'Three times a number' is 3n. The multiply sign is left out.
To evaluate, put the number in. If n is 4, then 3n + 5 is 17.
To solve n + 5 = 12, undo the +5 by taking 5 off both sides.

exercises.ask: If n = 4, what is 3n + 5?
exercises.why: 17. Three fours is 12, plus 5.

exercises.ask: Solve n + 5 = 12.
exercises.why: 7. Take 5 from both sides. Whatever you do to one side you do to the other.

exercises.ask: Solve 4n = 20.
exercises.why: 5. Divide both sides by 4.

exercises.ask: Solve n - 7 = 3.
exercises.why: 10. Add 7 to both sides to undo the subtraction.

exercises.ask: If n = 6, what is 2n - 4?
exercises.why: 8. Two sixes is 12, take away 4.

exercises.ask: 3n means 3 + n.
exercises.why: False. 3n means 3 times n. Writing them side by side always means multiply.

exercises.ask: A number doubled and then increased by 7 gives 25. What is the number?
exercises.hint: Write it as 2n + 7 = 25 and undo the steps backwards.
exercises.why: 9. Take 7 off both sides to get 2n = 18, then halve. Undo the last thing first.

topics.name: Area of Anything
topics.big: Cut it into rectangles and triangles.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.GR.2.1 and 2.2. Triangle area derived from the rectangle, then composite shapes by decomposing.

teach.text: A triangle is exactly half of a rectangle around it.

teach.cap: A 4 by 2 rectangle has area 8. A triangle inside it has area 4.

teach.text: So triangle area is base times height, halved.
For an odd shape, cut it into rectangles and triangles, work out each, and add.

exercises.ask: A rectangle 4 by 2. What is its area?
exercises.why: 8. Length times width.

exercises.ask: A triangle with base 4 and height 2. What is its area?
exercises.why: 4. Half of the 4 by 2 rectangle around it.

exercises.ask: A triangle with base 10 and height 6.
exercises.why: 30. Ten sixes is 60, halved.

exercises.ask: A triangle with base 7 and height 4.
exercises.why: 14. 28 halved. It works even when the halving lands on the other number.

exercises.ask: An L shape: a 5 by 3 rectangle plus a 2 by 2 square. Total area?
exercises.why: 19. 15 plus 4. Cutting a hard shape into easy ones is the whole method.

exercises.ask: Two triangles with the same base and height have the same area.
exercises.why: True, even if they look completely different. Lean one over as far as you like and the area does not change.

exercises.ask: A triangle has area 24 and base 8. What is its height?
exercises.hint: Work backwards: double the area first.
exercises.why: 6. Double 24 to get 48, then divide by the base of 8. Undoing the halving is the step people forget.

topics.name: Spread
topics.big: Where the middle is, and how spread out it is.
topics.parentNote: MA.6.DP.1.2 to 1.6. Mean, median, range and the box plot, plus how one changed value moves each of them.

teach.text: The median splits the data in half. Half above, half below.
A box plot shows the middle half as a box and the rest as whiskers.

teach.cap: Median 6, mean 8. One big value pulled the mean up but not the median.

teach.text: That is why house prices are usually reported as a median. A few enormous ones would wreck the mean.

exercises.ask: 2, 4, 6, 8, 20. What is the median?
exercises.why: 6, the middle of five values in order.

exercises.ask: 2, 4, 6, 8, 20. What is the mean?
exercises.why: 8. They add to 40, shared by 5. The mean is above four of the five numbers, dragged up by the 20.

exercises.ask: 2, 4, 6, 8, 20. What is the range?
exercises.why: 18. 20 take away 2. Range is easy to work out and easy to distort with one odd value.

exercises.ask: Change the 20 to 200. What is the median now?
exercises.why: 6, unchanged. The median only cares about position, not size, which is what makes it sturdy.

exercises.ask: Change the 20 to 200. What is the mean now?
exercises.why: 44. They add to 220, shared by 5. One value moved the mean by 36 and the median not at all.

exercises.ask: The median is affected less than the mean by one extreme value.
exercises.why: True. That is exactly why both get reported. If they disagree a lot, something unusual is in the data.

exercises.ask: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. What is the median of these six numbers?
exercises.hint: With an even count, take the middle two and find their midpoint.
exercises.why: 6, halfway between 5 and 7. With an even count the median often is not one of the numbers at all.
